sec.title: Introductions
sec.p: Gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis (GCPM) carries a poor prognosis, constrained by inadequate drug delivery, systemic toxicity, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. We developed E3C4, a single mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) co-encoding EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×41BB bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), to achieve localized dual-antigen T cell co-activation against GCPM.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: E3C4 was prepared by co-encapsulating m1Ψ-modified mRNAs using ionizable lipids. Functional characterization included surface plasmon resonance (SPR) for binding affinity, T cell-dependent cytotoxicity (TDCC), and 4–1BB reporter assays. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in PBMC-humanized mice bearing subcutaneous or orthotopic NCI-N87 tumors. Immune infiltration and cytokine release were analyzed via flow cytometry and ELISA. Safety was assessed in C57BL/6J mice through acute and repeated-dose toxicity studies.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Consequently, E3C4 exhibited optimal particle size and encapsulation efficiency. SPR confirmed high affinity for both BsAbs (KD ~10−10 M). Synergistic T cell activation achieved 80.9% cytotoxicity in vitro, significantly surpassing EpCAM×CD3 alone (29.1%, P<0.001). In subcutaneous models, 3 μg E3C4 induced 98.5% tumor growth inhibition with enhanced T cell infiltration and granzyme B expression. Intraperitoneal delivery enabled 96.4% tumor-localized expression, yielding superior efficacy over recombinant BsAbs in orthotopic models. E3C4 showed no mortality or cytokine release syndrome, with only transient elevations in IL-6, AST and ALT, as well as a >10% body weight loss that resolved within 2 weeks. The maximum tolerated dose exceeded the therapeutic dose by >200-fold.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: E3C4 constitutes a localized, synergistic platform that enables dual-antigen T cell co-activation within the peritoneal cavity. This approach maximizes antitumor efficacy while circumventing systemic toxicity, offering a novel immunotherapeutic strategy for GCPM.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Gastric Cancer (GC), a highly aggressive malignancy with global clinical relevance, has long remained among the leading causes of cancer-related incidence and mortality worldwide.1 Notably, data from GLOBOCAN 2023 (Global Cancer Statistics 2023) indicate that the annual number of newly diagnosed GC cases globally has surpassed 1 million, accompanied by approximately 769,000 annual deaths—collectively exerting an immense disease burden on healthcare systems and society at large.2 Within the current therapeutic framework for GC, Peritoneal Metastasis (PM) represents a pivotal bottleneck that constrains improvements in treatment efficacy: approximately 20% to 40% of patients with advanced GC develop PM, and these individuals exhibit exceedingly poor prognostic outcomes, with a median Overall Survival (OS) of only 3 to 6 months.3,4 Currently, both clinical treatment modalities and single-targeted strategies for GC-associated PM are plagued by substantial limitations: Systemic chemotherapy, the established first-line standard of care, fails to achieve therapeutic drug concentrations within peritoneal nodules due to the physiological barrier of the peritoneal cavity; furthermore, it frequently elicits severe systemic toxicities, including myelosuppression and gastrointestinal adverse events.5 Although local therapeutic approaches such as intraperitoneal chemotherapy and Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy (HIPEC) can enhance local drug concentrations to a certain degree, they are hindered by inherent drawbacks, such as short drug retention duration, heterogeneous lesion distribution, and a heightened risk of peritoneal adhesions. In the realm of targeted therapy, the clinical utility of anti-HER2 antibodies is limited by the low HER2 positivity rate (merely 15% to 20%) in GC.6 Additionally, immune checkpoint inhibitors are hampered by the robust immunosuppressive properties of the peritoneal Tumor Microenvironment (TME), resulting in an objective response rate of less than 15, leaving a profound unmet clinical need.7,8

From the standpoint of target discovery and translational research progress, EpCAM and Claudin18.2 represent the most clinically relevant and promising tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) in the context of GC and its peritoneal metastasis.9 Notably, EpCAM, as a transmembrane glycoprotein, is highly expressed in over 80% of primary GC lesions and 90% of peritoneal metastatic foci; critically, its expression level correlates positively with tumor invasive potential, lymph node metastatic burden, and the extent of peritoneal dissemination, thus rendering it an ideal broad-spectrum target for the selective targeting of peritoneal metastatic lesions.6,10 In contrast, Claudin18.2, a tight junction protein family member, demonstrates marked tissue specificity. While expression remains low and restricted to the apical membrane of gastric mucosal epithelial cells under normal physiological conditions, it becomes highly upregulated in a substantial proportion of gastric malignancies. Specifically, Claudin18.2 is overexpressed in approximately 50 to 60% of gastric cancer cases, with particularly prominent levels in the diffuse-type histological variant, and in about 70% of peritoneal metastatic lesions.11,12 Importantly, its expression status is tightly associated with adverse patient prognosis, thereby emerging as a key lineage-specific target for GC-directed targeted therapy.13 Nevertheless, T Cell Engager (TCE) antibodies against EpCAM or Claudin18.2 have failed to overcome existing clinical bottlenecks.14,15 This limitation not only delineates a crucial direction for the development of dual-target synergistic therapeutic strategies but also underscores the urgency of developing innovative therapeutic modalities characterized by “high specificity, low toxicity, and potent synergy” to improve the prognostic outcomes of patients with GC-associated peritoneal metastasis.

Effective T cell-mediated antitumor immune responses are contingent upon the synergistic activation of “the first signal (antigen-specific recognition signal) and the second signal (costimulatory signal)”.16 However, the clinical challenges encountered with current single-target CD3 bispecific TCEs explicitly reveal their core limitation: the lack of second signal activation. As prototypical TCEs, CD3 BsAbs transduce the first signal by bridging tumor-associated antigens and CD3 molecules on the T cell surface, thereby directing T cells to exert targeted cytotoxicity against tumor cells.17 Nevertheless, their application as monotherapies is constrained by two principal limitations.18 First, toxicity management presents a significant challenge. Systemically administered agents often achieve excessively high peak plasma concentrations, leading to nonspecific T cell activation. This promiscuous activation consequently provokes severe cytokine release syndrome, which has been reported to occur in over 30% of patients, as well as neurotoxicity.18 These adverse events necessitate dose reductions in clinical practice, ultimately compromising therapeutic efficacy. Second, the durability of therapeutic responses is suboptimal: T cells activated exclusively by the first signal are susceptible to rapid exhaustion within the immunosuppressive peritoneal TME, primarily due to the absence of costimulatory signals.18 This phenomenon manifests clinically as the “rapid emergence of drug resistance following an initial treatment response”.19

To address these unmet clinical challenges, the present study designed two BsAbs (EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×41BB) and established a synergistic therapeutic system featuring “dual-targeting plus dual-signal activation”. The core advantages of this system are delineated as follows: first, a synergistic and complementary targeting capability; second, synergistic signal activation. EpCAM exhibits coverage of over 80% of gastric cancer peritoneal metastatic lesions, thereby effectively mitigating the “escape from cytotoxicity” phenomenon observed in Claudin18.2-negative or low-expressing tumor cells.20 In contrast, the tissue specificity of Claudin18.2 offsets the potential off-target risk associated with low EpCAM expression in normal epithelial cells.21 Notably, the combined application of these two antibodies elevates targeting coverage to more than 95%, thus comprehensively overcoming the challenge of antigen heterogeneity in gastric cancer peritoneal metastasis. With respect to synergistic signal activation, EpCAM×CD3 serves as a “first signal provider”: it bridges EpCAM-positive tumor cells and CD3 molecules on the T cell surface, elicits antigen-specific T cell activation, directs T cell homing to tumor lesions, and initiates cytotoxic effects.22 In parallel, Claudin18.2×41BB acts as a “second signal amplifier”: it targets gastric cancer-specific tumor cells via Claudin18.2, while also engaging 4–1BB (a costimulatory receptor) on the surface of activated T cells to deliver critical costimulatory signals.23 This engagement drives robust T cell proliferation, enhances the secretion of key cytokines such as IFN-γ and TNF-α, and potently counteracts T cell exhaustion. Consequently, it amplifies antitumor immunity through two complementary mechanisms: the initiation of primary immune responses and the sustained maintenance of effector functions.

Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a robust delivery system for mRNA-mediated protein expression, characterized by high mRNA encapsulation efficiency, efficient endosomal escape for cytoplasmic translation, low immunogenicity due to ionizable lipid components, and tunable tissue tropism via surface modification, while also supporting scalable production and enabling rapid, transient protein expression without the risk of genomic integration, thus rendering them highly suitable for both basic research and clinical translation.24 A notable advantage of this platform lies in its ability to mediate sustained, low-level protein expression: it not only maintains a low peak plasma concentration to mitigate systemic toxicity but also ensures an optimal area under the curve (AUC) to guarantee therapeutic efficacy—attributes that are highly aligned with the pharmacokinetic requirements of TCE antibodies.25 Conventional recombinant TCEs often induce adverse events such as Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity due to excessively high Cmax, whereas mRNA-LNP-mediated local expression confines protein synthesis to the peritoneal cavity, substantially reducing the risk of systemic exposure.26 Furthermore, the capacity of mRNA-LNPs to co-deliver multiple mRNA molecules, as demonstrated in studies exploring the combined delivery of cytokines and immune checkpoint inhibitors, offers distinct technical advantages for synergistic dual-target TCE therapy.27 Traditional combination therapy with recombinant BsAbs requires separate drug manufacturing, quality control, and clinical trials, which are associated with challenges including high complexity in Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) and heavy regulatory burdens.28 In contrast, co-encapsulating mRNAs encoding the two BsAbs into a single LNP formulation classifies the product as a single drug entity, significantly simplifying the drug development process, shortening the clinical translation timeline, and providing inherent advantages during clinical filing.28

Herein, we report the development of E3C4, a single mRNA-LNP co-delivering EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×41BB BsAb-encoding mRNAs. This approach is designed to enable localized, dual-targeted T cell co-activation within the peritoneal cavity, aiming to overcome the limitations of current therapies by simultaneously enhancing efficacy and reducing systemic toxicity, with the potential to improve outcomes for patients with GC-associated PM.

sec.title: Experimental Materials
sec.p: Key materials required for cell culture, including high-glucose Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM,11965092), fetal bovine serum (FBS, A5256701), and penicillin-streptomycin (15140122), were all purchased from Gibco. For experimental assays, anti-His tag antibody (ab18184), recombinant human EpCAM protein (ab151338), human Claudin 18.2 protein (ab316081), human CD3E&D complex (ab286041), human 41BB protein (ab283931), and other routine test antibodies were acquired from Abcam. The human gastric cancer cell line NCI-N87 and Expi293F cells were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and Thermo Fisher Scientific, respectively. The Human TNFRSF9 (4–1BB) Reporter Jurkat Cell line was constructed in-house. Additional conventional reagents, such as 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) substrate solution (T0440), were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. The preparation of standard bispecific antibody proteins (EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin 18.2×41BB) and mRNA synthesis templates was commissioned to Nanjing GenScript Biotech Corporation. Restriction endonucleases, T4 DNA ligase, and T7 RNA polymerase used for in vitro transcription were purchased from New England Biolabs (NEB). 1-Methylpseudouridine-5′-triphosphate (1-meUTP, 1931922–77-8) was obtained from TriLink BioTechnologies. Lipid 5 (MCE, HY-138171, purity 99.78%), phosphatidylcholine, DMG-PEG (1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycero-3-methoxypolyethylene glycol, MCE, HY-112764, purity 98.4%), and cholesterol (MCE, HY-N0322, purity 99.4%), which were used for LNP encapsulation, were all purchased from MedChemExpress Technology. The peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were obtained from Shanghai Aoneng Biotechnology Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Miaoshun Biotechnology Co., Ltd. and all the processes of collection and separation comply with ethical requirements.

sec.title: Antibody Design and Preparation
sec.p: All antibody sequences (SEQs) were derived from public sources. Specifically, the sequences of 4–1BB and Claudin 18.2 were obtained from Givastomig, while the sequences of CD3 and EpCAM were derived from clone SP34 and Varsetatug, respectively. All sequences are mouse-derived humanized variants. The preparation of all newly designed antibody proteins in this study was performed by GenScript Biotech Corporation (Nanjing).

sec.title: In vitro Transcription of mRNA
sec.p: In vitro transcription of mRNA was performed using the constructed recombinant plasmids (in-house constructed) as templates. First, the recombinant plasmids were linearized via restriction endonuclease digestion. After verifying the integrity of linearization by agarose gel electrophoresis, the linearized plasmids were purified and recovered using the phenol-chloroform extraction method to remove residual circular plasmids, thereby ensuring the accuracy and integrity of subsequent transcription products. The in vitro transcription reaction was catalyzed by T7 RNA polymerase. Meanwhile, 1-methylpseudouridine-5′-triphosphate (1-meUTP) was added to the reaction system to replace conventional uridine triphosphate (UTP); this chemical modification enhances the in vivo stability of mRNA and reduces its immunogenicity. The transcription reaction was incubated at a constant temperature of 37°C for 4 hours. Upon completion of the reaction, DNase I was added to digest and remove the template DNA, thus terminating the transcription process. Purification of the transcription products was conducted in two steps: first, the MEGAClear RNA Purification Kit was used for preliminary purification to eliminate free nucleotides, enzyme proteins, and short nucleic acid fragments from the reaction system. Second, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was employed for fine purification using an Agilent 1260 Infinity II HPLC system equipped with an Agilent Zorbax SB-C18 column (4.6×250 mm, 5 μm). The chromatographic conditions were set as follows: mobile phase A was ultrapure water containing 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), and mobile phase B was acetonitrile containing 0.1% TFA; a gradient elution program was applied (0–5 min, 5% B; 5–20 min, 5–30% B; 20–25 min, 30–95% B) with a flow rate of 1 mL/min and a column temperature of 30°C. The target peak fractions were collected at a detection wavelength of 260 nm and subjected to lyophilization.

The integrity of the purified mRNA was analyzed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer with an RNA 6000 Nano Chip, requiring a RNA Integrity Number (RIN) ≥ 9.0. The capping efficiency of mRNA was determined using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Q Exactive HF-X liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) system equipped with a Thermo Scientific Accucore C18 column (2.1×150 mm, 2.6 μm). The mobile phase was a water-methanol system containing 0.1% formic acid, and the mass spectrometer was operated in the positive ion mode with an electrospray ionization (ESI) source. The capping efficiency was calculated based on the area ratio of characteristic ion peaks, ensuring a final mRNA capping efficiency ≥ 95%.

sec.title: LNP Encapsulation
sec.p: The mRNA-LNP formulation comprised the ionizable lipid Lipid 5, with the two mRNAs co-encapsulated at a 1:1 molar ratio. For the preparation process, first, the two mRNAs were mixed at the aforementioned molar ratio to form an aqueous solution, and the pH of this mixture was precisely adjusted to 4.0. Concurrently, phosphatidylcholine, Lipid 5, polyethylene glycol (PEG), and cholesterol were mixed at a molar ratio of 10:50:1.5:38.5 and fully dissolved in ethanol to prepare a lipid solution (N/P ratio is 6:1). Next, the pre-treated mRNA aqueous mixture and the lipid ethanol solution were rapidly mixed, and LNPs encapsulating the two mRNAs were formed via the self-assembly mechanism. After preparation, the encapsulation efficiency of LNPs was determined using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). A Zetasizer Nano ZS dynamic light scattering instrument (Malvern Panalytical) was employed to characterize the particle size and polydispersity index (PDI) of the prepared LNPs. Finally, the mRNA-LNP formulation with a concentration of 0.2 mg/mL was obtained and stored at 2–8°C for subsequent use.

sec.title: Cell Culture and mRNA Transfection
sec.p: The human embryonic kidney epithelial cell line Expi293F was cultured in suspension using Expi293™ Expression Medium under the conditions of 37°C, 8% CO2, and shaking at 125 rpm. Expi293F cells in the logarithmic growth phase were seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 1×106 cells/mL, with a total volume of 2 mL per well, and cultured until the cell viability reached over 95%. For transfection, different amounts of mRNA and 1–2 μL of Lipofectamine™ RNAiMAX transfection reagent were separately diluted in serum-free Opti-MEM medium, followed by incubation for 5 minutes each. The two diluted solutions were mixed and allowed to stand at room temperature for 15–20 minutes to form complexes. The complexes were gently added to the cell suspension, and the mixture was gently pipetted to ensure homogeneity. The cells were then incubated in a shaker at 37°C, 8% CO2, and 125 rpm for 4–6 hours. Subsequently, the medium was replaced with fresh Expi293™ Expression Medium, and the cells were further cultured for 48 hours before detecting the expression level of the target protein. The concentration of antibodies in the supernatant was accurately quantified using the sandwich ELISA method.

sec.title: Detection of the Targeted Protein Binding Activity of the BsAbs
sec.p: The binding affinity between the E3C4-encoding BsAbs in the cell culture supernatant and human target antigens was quantitatively determined using a Biacore T200 system based on the principle of SPR. The detailed procedure was as follows: A CM5 sensor chip was used, and the antigen was immobilized via amine coupling. First, the human target antigen was diluted to 5–10 μg/mL with 10 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 4.5). A mixture of 0.4 M 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide (EDC) and 0.1 M N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) was injected into the chip channel at a flow rate of 30 μL/min to activate the carboxyl surface for 10 minutes. Next, the antigen solution was injected to allow covalent binding of the target antigen to the activated groups on the chip surface via amino groups, with the immobilization level controlled to approximately 1000–2000 response units (RU). Finally, unreacted active sites were blocked with 1 M ethanolamine-HCl (pH 8.5) at a flow rate of 30 μL/min for 7 minutes. During the analysis run, HBS-EP+ buffer, containing 10 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, 3 mM EDTA, and 0.05% v/v surfactant P20, with pH 7.4, was used as the running buffer. The system temperature was set to 25°C, and the flow rate was maintained at 30 μL/min. The fusion antibodies were diluted with the running buffer to a series of concentrations: 3.125 nM, 6.25 nM, 12.5 nM, 25 nM, 50 nM, and 100 nM. These dilutions were injected into the antigen-immobilized channel and the blank control channel in ascending order of concentration. The association phase was maintained for 120 seconds, and the dissociation phase was extended to 300 seconds to fully observe the stability of the antibody-antigen complex. After each concentration cycle, the chip surface was immediately rinsed with 10 mM glycine-HCl buffer (pH 1.5) at a flow rate of 30 μL/min for 30 seconds to regenerate the antigen sites, followed by a 60-second equilibration period to ensure baseline stability. After collecting all sensorgrams, data processing was performed using Biacore T200 Evaluation Software. The response values from the blank channel and the buffer control signal were subtracted to eliminate interference from non-specific binding. A 1:1 Langmuir binding model was used for global fitting of the association-dissociation curves, and the equilibrium dissociation constant (KD value) between the fusion antibodies and human target antigens was calculated.

sec.title: Detection of the Tumor Cell Binding Activity of the BsAbs
sec.p: Flow cytometry was employed to determine the binding activity of the two BsAbs (expressed in cell supernatants) to NCI-N87 tumor cells. Briefly, NCI-N87 cells were resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) supplemented with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS), and the cell concentration was adjusted to 1×106cells/mL. A 100 μL aliquot of the cell suspension (corresponding to 1×105 cells) was transferred to a flow cytometry tube. Serial dilutions of each bispecific antibody were separately added to the tubes, followed by incubation at 4 °C for 1 hour to allow sufficient binding between the antibodies and target proteins on the cell surface. After incubation, the cells were washed three times with 2% FBS-supplemented PBS to remove unbound antibodies. Subsequently, an appropriate volume of fluorochrome-conjugated secondary antibody (goat anti-His tag-FITC, diluted at a ratio of 1:500) was added, and the mixture was incubated at 4 °C for 30 minutes in the dark. Unbound secondary antibody was removed by an additional three washes with 2% FBS-supplemented PBS. Finally, the cells were resuspended in 300 μL of 2% FBS-supplemented PBS and analyzed using a flow cytometer (BD FACSCanto II). The excitation wavelength was set to 488 nm, and the emission wavelength was set to 525 nm. The binding of BsAbs (from cell supernatants) to tumor cells was evaluated based on the detected fluorescence intensity.

sec.title: T Cell-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (TDCC) Assay
sec.p: NCI-N87-luc tumor target cells in the logarithmic growth phase were used. The original culture medium in the dish was aspirated, and 2 mL of 0.25% trypsin-EDTA solution was added. The cells were incubated at 37 °C for 3–5 minutes until complete detachment. Digestion was terminated by adding RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, and the cells were collected by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 5 minutes. After discarding the supernatant, the cells were resuspended in fresh complete medium. Viable cells were counted using trypan blue staining, and the cell concentration was adjusted to 2×105cells/mL. The cell suspension was stored at 4 °C for subsequent use. For the revival of cryopreserved PBMCs, the cryovial was removed from liquid nitrogen and immediately placed in a 37 °C water bath with gentle shaking until only a small amount of ice crystals remained. The cell suspension was transferred to a centrifuge tube containing 7 mL of pre-warmed RPMI 1640 medium and centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 10 minutes. After discarding the supernatant, the PBMCs were resuspended in complete medium, counted, and adjusted to a concentration of 7×105cells/mL. The PBMCs were equilibrated in a 37 °C, 5% CO2 incubator for 30 minutes before use. The assay was performed in a 96-well white luminescence detection plate with a total reaction volume of 100 μL per well. The components were added in the following order: 50 μL of target cell suspension (containing 1×104 cells), 40 μL of effector cell (PBMC) suspension (containing 2.8×104 cells, resulting in an effector-to-target [E:T] ratio of 3:1), and 10 μL of serially diluted drug solution. Meanwhile, control groups were set up as follows: blank control (50 μL medium + 50 μL effector cells), target cell control (50 μL target cells + 50 μL medium), and maximum lysis control (50 μL target cells + 50 μL 1% Triton X-100). Each group included three replicate wells. After sample addition, the side of the plate was gently tapped to mix the components (avoiding bubble formation), and the plate was incubated in a 37 °C, 5% CO2 humidified incubator for 48 hours. After incubation, 100 μL of room temperature-equilibrated Luciferase Assay Reagent was added to each well. The plate was incubated at room temperature for 10–15 minutes in the dark to ensure complete cell lysis and stable luminescent signals. A multimode microplate reader (eg, PerkinElmer EnVision) was used to measure the relative luminescence units (RLU) per well, with no filters set for excitation or emission light. The cytotoxicity rate was calculated using the following formula: Cytotoxicity rate (%) = [1 − (RLU of experimental well−RLU of blank control well)/(RLU of target cell control well − RLU of blank control well)] × 100.

sec.title: Human TNFRSF9 (4-1BB) Reporter Jurkat Cell Activation Assay
sec.p: NCI-N87 target cells in the logarithmic growth phase were digested with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA, and digestion was terminated with complete medium. The cells were collected by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 5 minutes, resuspended in RPMI 1640 complete medium supplemented with 10% FBS, and counted using trypan blue staining to ensure a viable cell rate ≥ 95%. The cell concentration was adjusted to 2×105cells/mL. A 100 μL aliquot of the cell suspension (containing 2×104 target cells per well) was seeded into a 96-well white luminescence detection plate. The plate was incubated overnight in a 37 °C, 5% CO2 humidified incubator to allow cell adhesion and reach 80–90% confluence. On the following day, the culture medium of target cells in each well was carefully aspirated to avoid damaging the adherent cells. Meanwhile, human TNFRSF9 (4–1BB) Reporter Jurkat effector cells were revived, resuspended in fresh complete medium, counted, and adjusted to a concentration of 4×106cells/mL. A 50 μL aliquot of the effector cell suspension (containing 2×105 effector cells per well, resulting in an E:T ratio of 10:1) was added to the detection plate. Subsequently, 50 μL of serially diluted Claudin18.2×4-1BB bispecific antibody was added to achieve the desired final concentrations. The plate was gently shaken to mix the components and incubated in a 37 °C, 5% CO2incubator for 6 hours to fully activate the reporter cell signaling pathway. Thirty minutes before the end of incubation, the GMOne-Step 2.0 Luciferase Reporter Gene Assay Kit was removed from −20 °C and thawed at room temperature in the dark, with gentle inversion 3–5 times during thawing. After incubation, 100 μL of the thawed assay reagent was added to each well, and the mixture was gently pipetted five times with a sterile pipette tip (to avoid bubble formation and cell damage). The plate was incubated at room temperature for 5 minutes in the dark to ensure complete cell lysis and sufficient reaction between luciferase and its substrate. A multimode microplate reader was used to measure the RLU per well.

sec.title: In vivo Expression Test of mRNA-LNPs in Mice
sec.p: Female M-NSG mice (6–8 weeks old) were used in this experiment and housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) environment throughout the study: temperature was controlled at (22±2) °C, humidity was maintained at (50±10)%, and a 12 h light/12 h dark circadian rhythm was maintained. Sterilized feed and sterile drinking water were provided, and bedding was changed twice weekly. Mice were acclimatized for 7 days, during which their physiological status was observed daily. Subsequently, mice were grouped using a random number table based on body weight to ensure no statistically significant difference in the average body weight between groups (P > 0.05).

In the single-dose administration experiment, mice were intraperitoneally injected via the tail vein with 3 μg or 10 μg of E3C4 (administered volume: 100 μL, diluted in sterile normal saline). Serum samples were collected before administration (0 h) and at 3 h, 6 h, 12 h, 24 h, 48 h, 72 h, 120 h, and 168 h post-administration. For each collection, mice were briefly anesthetized with 2–3% isoflurane, and 0.2–0.3 mL of blood was obtained from the retro-orbital venous plexus using a heparinized capillary tube. After the procedure, mice were monitored until full recovery from anesthesia. After coagulation, the blood was centrifuged at 3000 rpm at 4 °C for 10 minutes to separate serum, which was then stored at −80 °C until analysis.

In the repeated administration experiment, mice received a weekly intraperitoneal injection of 3 μg E3C4 (diluted as above). Serum samples were collected before each administration and at 12 h, 48 h, 72 h, and 168 h post-administration using the same method described above. The concentration of fusion proteins in serum was detected by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to analyze expression kinetics, with the detailed procedure as follows: EpCAM or Claudin 18.2 antigen was diluted to 2 μg/mL in carbonate buffer (pH 9.6), and a 96-well plate was coated with 100 μL of the diluted antigen per well, followed by incubation at 4 °C overnight. The next day, after washing with PBST (PBS containing 0.05% Tween-20), the plate was blocked with 5% non-fat milk at 37 °C for 1 hour. Serum samples (or standards) were added and incubated at 37 °C for 1.5 hours. After washing, HRP-conjugated anti-His tag secondary antibody (diluted 1:5000) was added and incubated at 37 °C for 1 hour. Finally, 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) substrate was added for color development, and the reaction was terminated with 2 M H2SO4. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a microplate reader, and the concentration of fusion proteins was calculated based on the standard curve.

sec.title: Efficacy Study in PBMC-Humanized NCI-N87 Subcutaneous Xenograft Model
sec.p: Female PBMC-humanized M-NSG mice (approximately 10 weeks old) were obtained from Biocytogen Pharmaceuticals (Beijing) Co., Ltd. and used in current study, with housing conditions referring to Section 2.10. NCI-N87 tumor cells in the logarithmic growth phase were digested with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA, and digestion was terminated with complete medium. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 100 g for 5 minutes, resuspended in RPMI 1640 complete medium supplemented with 10% FBS, and counted using trypan blue staining (viable cell rate ≥ 95%). The cell concentration was adjusted to 5×106 cells/mL, and 100 μL of the cell suspension was subcutaneously inoculated into the dorsal neck region of each mouse. Different treatment groups were established, including: NST mRNA-LNP (3 μg) group, EpCAM×CD3 protein (10 μg) group, Claudin18.2×41BB protein (20 μg) group, EpCAM×CD3 protein (10 μg) + Claudin18.2×41BB protein (20 μg) combination group (Protein combo, abbreviated as Pro combo), E3C4 (1 μg) group, and E3C4 (3 μg) group. The mRNA-LNP group was administered via tail vein injection once weekly (QW), while the protein groups were administered twice weekly (BIW). Tumor volume was measured using a vernier caliper by recording the longest tumor diameter (length) and the perpendicular shortest diameter (width). Tumor volume was calculated using the formula: Volume = length × width2 × 0.5. Changes in tumor volume were monitored and recorded. At the end of the experiment, mice were euthanized, and tumor tissues were excised, weighed, and recorded. Tumor weights were statistically analyzed across different groups.

After weighing the excised tumor tissues, the tissues were minced with sterile scissors and incubated in buffer containing collagenase in a constant-temperature shaker at 37 °C for a certain period (eg, 30–60 minutes) to ensure complete digestion. The digested tissues were then filtered through a 200-mesh cell sieve, and single-cell suspensions were collected by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 5 minutes. Red blood cells were removed using red blood cell lysis buffer, and the remaining cells were resuspended in PBS supplemented with 2% FBS and counted.

An appropriate amount of the single-cell suspension was incubated with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies against hCD45, hCD4, hCD8, Ki67, and Granzyme B at 4 °C for 30–60 minutes in the dark. After incubation, cells were washed twice with PBS to remove unbound antibodies, and finally resuspended in an appropriate volume of PBS for flow cytometry analysis. During detection, isotype control tubes were set to calibrate fluorescence signals, and at least 1×105 cell events were collected. Data were analyzed using flow cytometry software (eg, FlowJo) to calculate the proportions of hCD45+ cells, hCD45+hCD4+ cells, and hCD45+hCD8+ cells, as well as the proportions of Ki67+ proliferating cells and Granzyme B+ cells among hCD8+ cells. These parameters were used to evaluate the effects of different treatment groups on immune cell infiltration, activation, and function in the tumor microenvironment. All experimental procedures involving animals were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee with approved No.SL202408002.

sec.title: Efficacy Study in PBMC-Humanized NCI-N87 Orthotopic Xenograft Model
Tumor Model Establishment and Signal Detection
sec.p: Female PBMC-humanized M-NSG mice (approximately 10 weeks old) were obtained from Biocytogen Pharmaceuticals (Beijing) Co., Ltd. and used in current study, with housing conditions referring to Section 2.10. NCI-N87-luc tumor cells in the logarithmic growth phase were digested with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA, and digestion was terminated with complete medium. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 5 minutes, resuspended in RPMI 1640 complete medium supplemented with 10% FBS, and counted using trypan blue staining (viable cell rate ≥ 95%). The cell concentration was adjusted to 5×106 cells/mL. A sterile syringe was used to aspirate 0.2 mL of the pre-treated luciferase-labeled gastric cancer cell suspension, which was then intraperitoneally injected into the right abdominal region of each mouse (avoiding the liver area). After slow injection, the needle was retained for 3–5 seconds before withdrawal to prevent cell leakage. After inoculation, mice were placed in a warm environment for recovery and maintained under routine feeding conditions.

Ten to fifteen minutes before imaging, mice were anesthetized using 2–3% isoflurane inhalation and maintained on 1.5–2% isoflurane via a nose cone throughout the imaging procedure, followed by intraperitoneal injection (suitable for long-term monitoring, with slow luciferin release and sustained signals) or tail vein injection (suitable for rapid imaging, with signal peaks appearing at 5–10 minutes) of D-luciferin potassium salt (HY-12591A, MedChemExpress) at a dose of 150 mg/kg. After luciferin incubation, mice were fixed in a prone or supine position on the IVIS imaging platform (the supine position was more conducive to capturing intraperitoneal tumor signals and avoiding obstruction by dorsal tissues). An anesthesia maintenance system with 1.5% isoflurane was activated, and imaging parameters were set as follows: exposure time of 1–10 minutes (adjusted according to tumor size; longer exposure was used for early-stage tumors with weak signals), excitation wavelength of 570 nm, emission wavelength of 610 nm, and “high-resolution” mode. The imaging system was then initiated to collect fluorescence signals from the abdominal region of mice and generate 2D or 3D fluorescence images. The IVIS supporting software (eg, Living Image) was used to delineate the region of interest (ROI) within the abdominal cavity, and the total fluorescence flux within the ROI was calculated to quantify tumor growth.

sec.title: Tumor Signal Monitoring, Grouping, and Administration
sec.p: After tumor cell inoculation, in vivo small animal imaging was used to detect the fluorescence signals of mice in each group. These signals were used to characterize and compare changes in tumor size among groups and evaluate the anti-tumor effects of different treatments. The detailed operation was as follows: mice were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (50 mg/kg), and a heating pad was used to maintain the mice’s body temperature at 37 °C to ensure stable physiological status. Before imaging, the luciferin substrate D-luciferin (150 mg/kg) was injected via the tail vein; after entering the liver, this substrate produces detectable bioluminescent signals (wavelength: approximately 540–620 nm) under the catalysis of luciferase. The IVIS Spectrum software was used for noise reduction and pseudo-color processing of the original signals, converting luminescence/fluorescence intensity into pseudo-color images. Average fluorescence intensity or photon count (unit: Photons/s/cm2/sr) was then quantified for analysis.

Tumor-bearing mice were randomly grouped based on body weight and tumor signals, with 5 mice per group. The groups were administered NST mRNA-LNPs, 1 μg E3C4, 3 μg E3C4, and a combination of 10 μg EpCAM×CD3 and 20 μg Claudin18.2×41BB. All drugs were administered via intraperitoneal injection: mRNA-LNP drugs were administered once weekly, and protein drugs were administered twice weekly, with an injection volume of 100 μL per mouse. After administration, tumor signals and body weights of mice were recorded twice weekly, and the survival status of mice was recorded throughout the experiment.

sec.title: Preliminary Safety Assessment
sec.p: Female C57BL/6J mice (6–8 weeks old) were housed in an SPF environment (22±2 °C, 50±10% humidity, 12 h light/dark cycle) and acclimatized for 7 days before the experiment. The experiment was divided into two phases:

In the acute toxicity exploration phase, mice were randomly divided into a blank control group and multiple E3C4 dose groups (N=3). A single intraperitoneal injection was administered (100 μL per mouse, diluted in normal saline). Survival and physical signs were monitored for 7 days post-administration. Mice that died were dissected immediately, while surviving mice were euthanized on day 14 for gross anatomy. In the repeated tolerance confirmation phase, mice received tail vein injections of E3C4 on days 1, 8, 15, and 22, with a blank control group set up (N=5). Body weight and toxic side effects were monitored throughout the phase. In both the acute toxicity test and long-term toxicity test, changes in the organs of deceased mice were observed. If abnormal organ characteristics were observed, the corresponding tissues were fixed for subsequent pathological analysis. Serum levels of the cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits, while the activities of the liver enzymes aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were measured with standard automated biochemical analyzers.

sec.title: Animal Welfare, Anesthesia, and Euthanasia
sec.p: All animal procedures were strictly performed in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Academies Press, 8th edition, 2011) and approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Shenglun Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Approval No. SL2025010334). Efforts were made to minimize animal suffering and to use the minimum number of animals necessary for statistical validity.

Anesthesia: For invasive procedures such as retro-orbital blood collection, intraperitoneal tumor inoculation, and in vivo imaging, mice were anesthetized using 2–3% isoflurane in oxygen delivered via a precision vaporizer. The depth of anesthesia was monitored by the absence of pedal withdrawal reflex. During imaging sessions, anesthesia was maintained with 1.5–2% isoflurane using a nose cone connected to an anesthesia machine.

Euthanasia: At the experimental endpoints (eg, tumor volume exceeding 1500 mm3, severe clinical signs of distress, or as scheduled), mice were humanely euthanized. The primary method was carbon dioxide (CO2) asphyxiation in a gradually filled chamber (displacement rate of 30–70% of the chamber volume per minute), followed by secondary physical confirmation such as cervical dislocation. This method is consistent with the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals (2020 edition). For terminal blood collection or tissue harvest under deep anesthesia, euthanasia was achieved by cardiac exsanguination following profound anesthesia induced by an intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg). All personnel performing euthanasia were thoroughly trained.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All experimental data were obtained from at least 3 independent repeated experiments and expressed as “mean ± standard deviation (mean ± SD)”. GraphPad Prism 8.4 software was used for data processing and graphing. For in vivo experiments, mouse-related parameters (eg, tumor volume, body weight, fluorescence signal intensity) were statistically analyzed using t-tests or analysis of variance (ANOVA) based on data types. In statistical tests, a P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Construction of Lipid Nanoparticle E3C4 and Its Encoded Bispecific Antibody Proteins
sec.p:
E3C4 is a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation that generated by co-encapsulating two distinct m1Ψ modified mRNAs with ionizable lipids, with one mRNA encoding the EpCAM×CD3 BsAb and the other encoding the Claudin18.2×41BB BsAb (Figure 1A). This design strategy addresses the limitations of complex CMC processes associated with traditional BsAb drugs, thereby clearly emphasizing the technical innovation and application advantages of the “single-drug, dual-antibody” concept. Characterization results demonstrated that the prepared E3C4 particles exhibited a uniform particle size, with an average diameter of approximately 80 nm and encapsulation efficiency exceeding 95%. To further clarify the molecular binding properties of the BsAbs for the fundamental construction of E3C4, we first evaluated the antigen-binding activity at the protein level. Using SPR technology, we quantitatively assessed the binding kinetics and affinity of both EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×41BB BsAbs toward their respective targets. As shown in Figure 1B, the dissociation constant (Kd) of EpCAM×CD3 BiTE for human EpCAM and human CD3 protein was 4.51×10−10 M and 1.15×10−9 M, respectively. For Claudin18.2×41BB BiTE, the Kd value for human Claudin18.2 and 4–1BB protein was 5.51×10−10 M and 6.16×10−10 M, respectively. These data indicate that both two BsAbs possess extremely high tumor antigen-binding affinity, which ensures their efficient binding to tumor cells, and also appropriate binding to T cells under physiological conditions, laying a critical molecular foundation for the subsequent exertion of functional activity. Figure 1

In vitro cellular experiments were further conducted to confirm that the mRNAs loaded in E3C4 could be efficiently translated and assembled into two TCEs, which retains structural and functional integrity. First, we conducted in vitro cellular assays where Expi293F cells were transfected with varying doses (0.5–4.5 μg) of EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×41BB mRNAs, either alone or in combination; ELISA quantification of culture supernatants (Figure 2A–C) showed dose-dependent increases in BsAb expression, confirming efficient, regulatable translation of target antibodies by E3C4 mRNA. Functional evaluations using these antibody-containing supernatants demonstrated that for EpCAM×CD3, there was concentration-dependent enhancement of T cell-mediated cytotoxicity against EpCAM-positive tumor cells (Figure 2D) and increased binding between NCI-N87 gastric cancer cells and Jurkat T cells—with no significant difference versus recombinant EpCAM×CD3 protein (Figure 2E and F), while for Claudin18.2×41BB, there was concentration-dependent activation of 4–1BB reporter gene expression and enhanced binding between NCI-N87 cells and CD3/CD28-activated primary T cells, which consistents with recombinant Claudin18.2×41BB protein activity (Figure 2G–I), collectively confirming that mRNA-encoded EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×41BB BsAbs retain tumor cell-dependent functional activity with profiles comparable to their recombinant counterparts. (A–C) ELISA quantification of (A) EpCAM×CD3, (B) Claudin18.2×41BB, and (C) both BsAbs following transfection of Expi293F cells with increasing doses of the respective mRNAs. (D–F) Functional analysis of EpCAM×CD3 BsAb: (D) T cell-dependent cytotoxicity (TDCC) against NCI-N87 cells, (E) binding to NCI-N87 tumor cells, and (F) binding to Jurkat T cells. (G–I) Functional analysis of Claudin18.2×41BB BsAb: (G) activation of a 4–1BB reporter Jurkat cell line, (H) binding to NCI-N87 cells, and (I) binding to pre-activated primary human T cells. (K) Synergistic cytotoxicity assay where a fixed concentration of EpCAM×CD3 conditioned media was combined with increasing concentrations of Claudin18.2×41BB conditioned media. Data are mean ± SD (N=3).

We further investigated the synergistic antitumor effect of the two mRNA-encoded BsAbs using NCI-N87 cells, with the experimental design and mechanism of action shown in Figure 2J. The EpCAM×CD3 bispecific antibody mediates specific binding between T cells and tumor cells, thereby providing the first signal for T cell activation; the Claudin18.2×41BB bispecific antibody activates the 4–1BB pathway to deliver a co-stimulatory signal, namely the second signal for T cell activation. Their synergy significantly enhances T cell activation levels and antitumor function, confirming that the inclusion of the Claudin18.2×41BB bispecific antibody boosts the cytotoxic activity of the EpCAM×CD3 bispecific antibody. Experimental results showed that with the increase in the concentration of Claudin18.2×41BB bispecific antibody, the synergistic cytotoxic effect of the two BsAbs on cancer cells exhibited a concentration-dependent enhancement trend (Figure 2K). Notably, the tumor cell cytotoxicity rate of the synergistic group reached 80.9%, which was significantly higher than the 29.1% of the EpCAM×CD3 BsAb alone group (P < 0.001), fully demonstrating that the two antibodies have significant synergistic anti-tumor potential.

sec.title: In vivo Expression and Functional Validation of E3C4
sec.p:
We next assessed the pharmacokinetic profiles of EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×4-1BB BsAbs expressed in mice following administration of E3C4. A single dose (3 or 10 μg) led to rapid BsAb accumulation, with peak serum concentrations reached within 12 hours, followed by slow clearance over 168 hours (Figure 3A). As expected, the 10 μg dose resulted in significantly greater systemic exposure than the 3 μg dose, demonstrating dose-dependent and sustained expression typical of mRNA-LNP platforms (Figure 3B and C). Serum from treated mice exhibited potent, dose-dependent functional activity: EpCAM×CD3 BsAb mediated cytotoxicity against EpCAM-positive cells, while Claudin18.2×4-1BB BsAb activated a 4–1BB reporter system (Figure 3D and E). Importantly, these functional responses were comparable to those induced by recombinant protein controls, confirming the biological integrity of the mRNA-encoded BsAbs. Figure 3
E3C4 enables sustained in vivo production of functional bispecific antibodies. (A) Schematic of the single-dose E3C4 administration and blood sampling timeline. (B and C) Serum concentration-time profiles of (B) EpCAM×CD3 and (C) Claudin18.2×41BB bispecific antibodies following a single intraperitoneal dose of E3C4 (3 or 10 μg). (D and E) Functional activity of serum-derived (D) EpCAM×CD3 (T cell-dependent cytotoxicity) and (E) Claudin18.2×41BB (4–1BB reporter activation) compared to recombinant protein standards. (F and G) Pharmacokinetic profiles of both bispecific antibodies over three weeks of repeated E3C4 administration (3 μg, weekly). Data are mean ± SD (N=5). The dotted lines denote the baseline.

In repeat-dosing studies, animals received 3 μg E3C4 weekly for three weeks (Figure 3F). Both BsAbs showed consistent peak concentrations after each administration, followed by gradual clearance (Figure 3G). This profile—marked by delayed peak attainment, low Cmax, and sustained high AUC—aligns well with optimal pharmacokinetics for T cell engagers (TCEs). Together, these data support mRNA-LNPs as a promising delivery platform for TCEs, enabling reduced dosing frequency without compromising efficacy.

sec.title: E3C4 Demonstrates Superior Antitumor Efficacy in a PBMC-Humanized Model
sec.p:
To evaluate the antitumor efficacy of E3C4, we utilized a PBMC-humanized NSG mouse model bearing subcutaneous NCI-N87 tumors, comparing E3C4 against individual BsAbs and their recombinant protein combination (Pro combo) (Figure 4A). E3C4 treatment resulted in potent, dose-dependent tumor growth inhibition (TGI). The 3 μg dose of E3C4 achieved near-complete tumor regression (98.5% TGI at day 28), representing the most potent effect observed and significantly outperforming the EpCAM×CD3 monoprotein group (57.5% TGI, P < 0.05) (Figure 4B and C). Although the Pro combo was more effective than either monoprotein alone, it was still significantly less effective than the 3 μg E3C4 dose (P < 0.05), underscoring the superiority of the mRNA-LNP co-delivery platform. (B) Tumor growth curves and (C) final tumor weights of subcutaneous NCI-N87 xenografts. (D) Quantification of tumor-infiltrating human CD45+ (hCD45+) T cells. Proportions of Granzyme B+ (E) and Ki67+ (F) cells among hCD45+CD8+ T cells. Serum levels of IL-6 (G), IFN-γ (H), and TNF-α (I) measured 24 h after the first dose. Data are presented as mean ± SD. In Figure 4C–I #P < 0.05, ##P < 0.01, ###P < 0.001; *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01 vs EpCAM×CD3 group; ns, not significant (P > 0.05). N = 5 for tumor volume, weight and immune cell and cytokine analysis.

Analysis of tumor-infiltrating immune cells revealed the mechanistic basis for this enhanced efficacy. Tumors from the 3 μg E3C4 group exhibited significantly increased infiltration of human CD45+ T cells, along with higher frequencies of proliferating (Ki67+) and cytotoxic (Granzyme B+) CD8+ T cells compared to all other groups, including the Pro combo (Figure 4D–F). This suggests that the sustained, coordinated expression of both BsAbs by E3C4 creates a more robust and durable T-cell response within the tumor microenvironment. Consistent with the favorable pharmacokinetic profile of E3C4 (characterized by sustained exposure and low Cmax), cytokine analysis revealed a markedly improved safety profile. Despite its superior efficacy, the 3 μg E3C4 group induced significantly lower levels of key inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and TNF-α) at 24 hours post-dose compared to the Pro combo (Figure 4G–I). This critical finding indicates that the mRNA-LNP platform successfully uncouples efficacy from toxicity, mitigating the risk of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) associated with high peak concentrations of recombinant T cell engagers.

sec.title: Validation of Intraperitoneal Targeting and Efficacy in Orthotopic Intraperitoneal Tumor Model
sec.p:
To validate the tumor-targeting capability of our LNP platform, we first administered luciferase-encoding mRNA-LNPs—identical in composition to E3C4—via intraperitoneal injection in an orthotopic gastric cancer model. Bioluminescent imaging revealed highly specific accumulation within the peritoneal tumor microenvironment, with 96.4% of the total signal localized to ascitic fluid (83.7%) and gastrointestinal tissues (12.7%), and minimal distribution to distant organs (Figure 5A and B). This result strongly suggests that E3C4 would achieve similarly targeted expression at malignant sites. Figure 5
Investigation of mRNA-LNP distribution and targeting in a murine intraperitoneal tumor model. (A) Treatment schedule for the in vivo biodistribution study; (B) In vivo imaging images and statistical analysis of tissue quantification data. N = 5 for each group.

We next evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of E3C4 in this model. While the recombinant protein combination (Pro combo) showed initial activity comparable to E3C4 within the first 10 days, its efficacy plateaued and was significantly surpassed by both the 1 μg and 3 μg E3C4 doses by day 24 (Figure 6A–C). The superior performance of E3C4, particularly at the lower dose where its exposure was less pronounced in the subcutaneous model, can be attributed to the enhanced local concentration facilitated by the favorable biodistribution of intraperitoneal LNPs. This creates a high effective dose precisely within the tumor-bearing compartment, enabling potent and sustained T-cell activation. Consistent with this premise and the favorable pharmacokinetics of mRNA-LNPs, E3C4 treatment resulted in a markedly improved cytokine safety profile. Serum levels of IL-6 were significantly lower in both E3C4 dose groups compared to the Pro combo group after the final injection (Figure 6D, P < 0.01 and P < 0.05 for 1μg and 3μg group, respectively), demonstrating that the potent antitumor efficacy of E3C4 is achieved without inducing a commensurate CRS risk. sec.title: Preliminary Safety Assessment of E3C4 in Mice
sec.p:
The safety profile of E3C4 was evaluated in healthy C57BL/6J mice. In an acute toxicity study, a single intraperitoneal dose of up to 10 mg/kg caused no mortality, with transient body weight reduction (12.5–26.5%) observed (Table 1). Given that the minimum effective dose (MED) in efficacy models was below 0.05 mg/kg, the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) exceeded the MED by at least 200-fold. In a repeat-dose study, administration of 10 mg/kg E3C4 weekly for four weeks was well-tolerated with no mortality. It is worth noting that although no animals died, their weight dropped by more than 25%, indicating a relatively obvious toxicity in their bodies. All of them recovered two weeks after the last administration. Transient elevations in IL-6, AST, and ALT levels were observed shortly after the first dose but returned to baseline by one week after the final administration (Figure 7). Taken together, our results confirm that E3C4 has an acceptable safety profile; while obvious body weight loss indicative of toxicity occurred in healthy mice, its general tolerability combined with a low effective dose yields a sufficiently broad therapeutic window.Table 1

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Gastric cancer with peritoneal metastasis (GCPM) remains a formidable clinical challenge because current treatments, such as immune checkpoint blockers (ICBs) and bispecific TCE, have demonstrated limited efficacy. ICBs achieve response rates of less than 15% in GCPM patients, largely due to the profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment,6,29 while targeted modalities such as the EpCAM×CD3 bispecific antibody, catumaxomab, though exhibiting preliminary activity, are constrained by systemic toxicity and modest efficacy in clinical trials.22

In response, we developed E3C4, an innovative mRNA-LNP formulation co-encoding EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×41BB BsAbs, which represents a multimodal strategy designed to overcome these limitations through dual-target coverage, dual-signal activation, and localized delivery. The ionizable lipid used in this study is Lipid 5, a well-established lipid for mRNA-based protein replacement therapy with its safety and efficacy fully validated in numerous preclinical and clinical studies.30,31 The co-encapsulation of two distinct mRNA species within a single LNP formulation ensures synchronized expression of both BsAbs, which is critical for achieving synergistic T-cell activation. The EpCAM×CD3 bispecific antibody acts as a “signal I provider”, which can precisely bridge EpCAM-positive tumor cells and T cells to trigger antigen-specific activation. The Claudin18.2×41BB bispecific antibody, designated as a “signal II amplifier”, binding 4–1BB on activated T cells to promote proliferation (increased Ki67+CD8+T cells) and enhance cytokine secretion (eg, IFN-γ). Our results demonstrate that the combination of EpCAM×CD3 and Claudin18.2×4-1BB BsAbs enhances T cell cytotoxicity while reducing exhaustion. This synergistic effect was validated in vitro, with the combined bispecific antibody group exhibiting a significantly higher tumor cytotoxicity rate (80.9%) compared to the EpCAM×CD3 monotherapy group (29.1%). Another key translational advantage of E3C4 lies in the mRNA-LNP platform itself. First, it simplifies the complex Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) processes typically associated with combination therapies by encapsulating two therapeutic mRNAs within a single entity.28 Second, and most critically, it enables a favorable pharmacokinetic (PK) profile characterized by sustained, low-level expression in vivo. Unlike recombinant proteins that often cause cytokine release syndrome (CRS) due to high peak concentrations (Cmax), E3C4 administration resulted in gradual protein accumulation and prolonged exposure (high AUC), as shown in Figure 3. This PK profile directly correlated with improved safety; E3C4 induced only transient and mild elevations of IL-6, in stark contrast to the pronounced cytokine release observed with the recombinant protein combination (Pro combo) (Figures 4G–I and 6D).

The sustained and localized expression paradigm of E4C3 is pivotal to explaining E3C4’s superior efficacy. In the subcutaneous model, the 3 μg E3C4 dose achieved near-complete tumor regression (98.5% TGI), outperforming the Pro combo. We attribute this advantage not merely to the presence of both BsAbs, but to the continuous signaling enabled by mRNA-LNPs. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that the 3 μg E3C4 group exhibited the highest levels of T-cell infiltration, proliferation (Ki67+), and cytotoxicity (Granzyme B+) (Figure 4D–F). This suggests that persistent “Signal 1 + Signal 2” activation within the tumor microenvironment effectively counteracts T-cell dysfunction, a benefit that intermittent protein injections cannot provide. Moreover, the efficacy of intraperitoneal (i.p.) therapy for GCPM is highly dependent on local biodistribution. Our tracking study using luciferase mRNA-LNPs, which share an identical formulation with E3C4, provided a compelling mechanistic insight: 96.4% of the signal was localized to the peritoneal compartment (ascites and GI tissues) (Figure 5). This highly favorable distribution pattern directly explains the potent efficacy of E3C4 in the orthotopic model. It ensures that the encoded BsAbs are produced predominantly at the disease site, maximizing local anti-tumor activity while minimizing systemic exposure and off-target toxicity, a significant improvement over conventional intraperitoneal chemotherapy.23

The safety profile of LNP-formulated E3C4 was assessed in healthy C57BL/6J mice. No mortality was observed following a single intraperitoneal administration at doses up to 10 mg/kg. With the minimum effective dose (MED) < 0.05 mg/kg, the MTD exceeded the MED by at least 200-fold. Weekly 10 mg/kg injections for 4 consecutive weeks also caused no mortality; the >25% body weight reduction, a hallmark of systemic toxicity linked to LNP-mediated off-target effects on metabolic tissues, signaled overt biological perturbation. Notably, complete weight recovery was achieved 2 weeks post the final treatment, implying that this toxicity was transient and reversible rather than cumulative or irreversible. Transient elevations in IL-6, AST and ALT levels detected after the initial dose normalized 1 week post the last injection (Figure 7). Collectively, these findings confirm that LNP-E3C4 exhibits an acceptable safety profile: despite dose-dependent weight loss indicative of acute toxicity, the absence of mortality and robust post-treatment recovery demonstrates that animals tolerate high-dose exposure, conferring a favorable therapeutic window.

While our findings highlight the promising efficacy and safety profile of E3C4, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the use of immunodeficient NSG mice reconstituted with human PBMCs may not fully recapitulate the complex human immune microenvironment. Future studies employing humanized mouse models with endogenous immune systems or patient-derived xenografts (PDX) could provide more translational relevance. Second, although EpCAM and Claudin18.2 cover >95% of GC PM cases, antigen-negative subtypes may still evade therapy. Exploring additional targets or combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors could further broaden applicability. Third, the safety assessment in C57BL/6J mice, which lack the fully human targets (EpCAM, Claudin18.2, CD3, 4–1BB), precludes a complete evaluation of potential on-target, off-tumor toxicity. More relevant models expressing human targets are necessary for comprehensive safety profiling. Furthermore, while acute and repeated-dose studies showed favorable safety, long-term toxicity and immunogenicity of repeated mRNA-LNP administration remain to be evaluated. Finally, scale-up production, stability, and GMP-compliant manufacturing of dual-mRNA LNPs warrant further optimization. Phase I trials should prioritize intraperitoneal administration and biomarker-driven patient selection.

Looking forward, the modular nature of the E3C4 platform holds great potential. It could be adapted to target other antigen pairs in GCPM or other peritoneal malignancies (eg, ovarian cancer). Moreover, the platform could be further armed with mRNAs encoding immunomodulators (eg, cytokines) to enhance T-cell persistence and memory formation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, our study demonstrates that intraperitoneal delivery of E3C4 represents a novel and potent immunotherapeutic strategy for GCPM. By leveraging the mRNA-LNP platform for the localized and sustained co-expression of two synergistic BsAbs, E3C4 successfully integrates the advantages of dual-target coverage, dual-signal activation, and favorable biodistribution. This approach effectively addresses the dual challenges of insufficient efficacy and systemic toxicity associated with current therapies, offering a promising new avenue for treating this devastating condition.
